   CITY OF BEVERLY HILLS

  POLICY AND MANAGEMENT

  MEMORANDUM

 TO:  City Council Liaison/Legislative/Lobby Committee

 FROM:  Mandy Jiang, Senior Management Analyst

 DATE:  September 29, 2026

 SUBJECT:  Staff Memorandum – Summary of Propositions 1, 43, and 45

 ATTACHMENT:  1. Lobbyist Memo for Each Proposition

INTRODUCTION
This report provides a snapshot summary of the legislative bills brought forth to the City Council
Liaison Legislative / Lobby Committee for consideration. Included in this summary is any relevant
language from the City’s 2025 Legislative Platform that may provide nexus for recommending a
position. Verbal overview will be provided by Shaw Yoder Antwih Schmelzer & Lange (SYASL).
The attachment to this report includes memos for each proposition detailing bill provisions,
author’s intent, and those in support or opposition.

After discussion of each proposition, the Liaisons may recommend the following actions:
1) Oppose; 2) Support; 3) Support if amended; 4) Oppose unless amended; 5) Remain neutral;
6) Provide other direction to City staff. Should the Liaisons recommend the City take a position
on a bill, staff will place the item on a future City Council agenda for concurrence.

DISCUSSION

1. Proposition 1 – AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS.
  LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
  
  Summary: Proposition 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in state general obligation
  bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing,
  mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable
  housing, and downpayment assistance.
  
  Fiscal Impact: If passed, will allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund
  various affordable housing programs. If passed, State costs will increase by $500
  million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.1
   Comment: The City took a position of Support if Amended on a housing bond bill last
  year, AB 736 (Wicks) which was ultimately repurposed for another matter and didn’t
  pass out of committee. In the position letter addressed to the bill author, the City
  requested a change in bill text to allow the bond dollars flow to qualified regional or
  local organizations such as LACAHSA and SCAG, rather than to the State’s Housing
  and Community Development Department (HCD).
   Legislative Platform Nexus: Aligns with the legislative priority, “Support legislation
  which encourages the use of federal and state incentives for local government action
  rather than mandates.”

1 prop1-110326.pdf
 2.  Proposition 43 - LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL
  GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
   Summary: Proposition 43 would raise the voter threshold from a simple majority to
  two-thirds for all local special taxes, whether the measure is placed on the ballot by a
  local governing body or through the local initiative process. Effective beginning
  January 1, 2027, this would apply to any special local tax (e.g., sales taxes for specific
  purpose, utility tax) being imposed, extended, or increased. The measure would also
  prohibit a local government, including its electorate acting through the initiative power,
  from imposing an ad valorem tax on real property except as permitted under existing
  constitutional provisions.
   Fiscal Impact: Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain
  taxes. As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than
  they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend
  on future decisions by local governments and voters. 2
   Comment: Examples of local special tax revenue use may include specifically funding
  public safety response (a city special sales tax to fire protection and/or police
  response), schools (parcel tax), affordable housing (LA County Measure A),
  healthcare services (LA County Measure ER).
   Legislative Platform Nexus: Aligns with the legislative priorities:
  o “Oppose legislation that would undermine voter-approved initiatives to
  guarantee ongoing revenue sources for the City of Beverly Hills.”
  o “Oppose legislation that would preempt the City’s authority over local taxes
  and fees.”

3.  Proposition 45 – MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN
  PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
   Summary: Proposition 45 would limit reviews under CEQA. Placed on the ballot by
  the California Chamber of Commerce, Prop 45 aims to help developers advance
  projects they designate as “essential” more quickly and easily. It would impose a 365-
  day limit on environmental reviews for those projects, including infrastructure like
  roads and bridges, housing, schools, broadband and wildfire mitigation. It would also
  require courts to rule within 270 days on lawsuits related to the environmental review
  law.3 However, it should be noted that the text of this measure defining those projects
  are broad.
   Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of
  millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by
  developer fees. Longer-term, potentially more significant fiscal impact uncertain.4
   Comment: Staff concerns regarding continued piecemeal erosion of CEQA through
  project-specific exemptions and alternative procedures. The cumulative effect after
  several years of this type of legislation is an increasingly complicated patchwork of
  rules that makes CEQA more difficult for local agencies to interpret and administer.
  Proposition 45 would add another layer of procedures, deadlines, and limitations for a
  broad range of projects. City will have tighter deadlines to review utility projects, and
  also less time to comment on external agencies’ proposed utility projects impacting
  city infrastructure.

2  prop43-110326.pdf
3 CA voter guide: Prop. 45 on speeding environmental reviews

  the City of Beverly Hills’ local authority whether by state or federal legislation or ballot

RECOMMENDATION
After discussion of each proposition, the Liaisons may recommend the following actions:
   Oppose
   Support
   Support if amended
   Oppose unless amended
   Remain neutral; or
   Provide other direction to City staff.

Should the Liaisons recommend the City take a position on a proposition, staff will then place the
item on a future City Council agenda for concurrence. If Liaisons recommend differing positions
on a piece of legislation, the item will be taken to a City Council Study Session for establishment
of a position.

Re:  Proposition 1 Memo

Path to the Ballot
Proposition 1 was placed on the ballot though SB 417 (Limón) as a legislatively referred
bond measure. Legislatively referred bond measures require a two-third majority vote and a
governor’s signature.

The bill, SB 417, was originally introduced in the Senate by Senator Cabaldon in February of
2025, with another housing bond bill, AB 736, introduced in the Assembly by
Assemblymember Wicks. The two measures were similar in scope of funding all the same
programs and both being a $10 billion a3ordable housing bond. The di3erences were in
allocations in funding, where SB 417 allocated more funds in the Multihousing Family
Program, wildﬁre prevention, rental assistance, and a3ordable housing construction
program, but less allocation for the Joe Serna Jr. Farmworker Housing Program. Ultimately,
only SB 417 proceeded to the governor’s desk, and through a three-party agreement between
the Assembly, Senate, and the Governor, the bill’s scope was expanded to increase the bond
authorization by $1.25 billion for the Department of Veteran A3airs Home Loan Program.

SB 417 was signed by the Governor on June 25, 2026. On June 29th, the Secretary of State
designated the bond as Proposition 1 for the upcoming November 3rd ballot.

Summary
The initiative would authorize $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds to fund various
a3ordable housing programs. Of that total amount, $1.25 billion would go toward veteran
housing, while the rest would fund rental homes, homeownership programs, farmworker
housing, a3ordable student housing, tribal housing and more. The bond is expected to help
fund up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, while also helping another 40,000 households buy
a home.
 The proceeds would be allocated as follows:

    $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing through low-interest loans to
  local governments or private developers with a requirement that units are reserved
  for low-income households for 55 years and a portion of the funding used for
  supportive housing that provides mental health or substance abuse counseling;

    $1.1 billion for homeownership loan programs and housing development for low- and
  moderate- income households;

    $500 million for infrastructure projects, such as water, sewage, parks, and
  transportation;

    $450 million for loans or grants for farmworker housing;

    $350 million for student housing, split evenly between University of California and
  California State University;

    $200 million for grants to tribes for housing projects; and

    $200 million for local governments developing pilot projects to reduce housing costs.

From: Andrew K. Antwih, Partner, Shaw Yoder Antwih Schmelzer & Lange
  Dylan Hoffman, Legislative Advocate, Shaw Yoder Antwih Schmelzer & Lange

Re:  Proposition 43 Memo

Summary
The initiative would amend the California Constitution to require that local ballot measures
proposing, extending, or increasing special taxes initiated by citizens receive a two-thirds
(66.67%) vote to be enacted.

Currently, local special tax measures can be enacted in two ways: 1) a local governing board
sends the tax to voters, and it is approved by a two-thirds vote, or 2) citizens can petition to
place a special tax on local ballots, and it is approved by a simple majority of voters.

The initiative would also prohibit any local government from levying ad valorem taxes on real
property, including by ballot initiative, except for those authorized under Article XIII and
Article XIII A, which establishes a 1% base tax on real property and authorizes additional
voter-approved bond debt-service property taxes.

Path to the Ballot
In California state law, the core di+erence between a statewide ballot initiative and a
legislatively initiated ballot measure (often called a legislative referral) lies in how they
originate and qualify for the ballot. A ballot initiative bypasses the state government to be
driven entirely by citizens, whereas a legislatively initiated measure must be passed by the
California State Legislature before going to the voters.

Proposition 43 is a legislative referral. Proposition 43 was placed on the ballot as part of a
legislative compromise between Democratic state leaders and petitioners sponsoring
another initiative, the Local Taxpayer Protection Act, that would have increased the vote
requirement to pass citizen-initiated local special taxes from a simple majority to a two-
thirds vote; prohibited charter cities from imposing their own real estate transfer taxes,
whether for general or speciﬁc purposes, above the existing statutory rate of $0.275 per $500
of value; and invalidated any property-related special taxes previously adopted with an
approval rate below two-thirds or real estate transfer taxes in charter cities. Proposition 43
is not retroactive like the withdrawn ballot initiative.
 California state law allows initiative sponsors to withdraw qualiﬁed initiatives until the ballot
ﬁnalization deadline, which is 131 days before the election. he initiative, the Local Taxpayer
Protection Act, was withdrawn from the ballot after the California State Legislature passed
Proposition 43 on June 25 — the 2026 ballot ﬁnalization deadline. It passed the state
Assembly by a vote of 68-2, with nine not voting. It passed the state Senate by a vote of 35-1,
with four not voting.

The Local Taxpayer Protection Act, sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association,
along with other business and taxpayer organizations, arises out of a 2017 California
Supreme Court decision. On August 28, 2017, the California Supreme Court entered a
decision in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland, 3 Cal. 5th 924, which held that
California Constitution Article XIIIC, Section Two, subdivision (b)’s requirement that general
taxes be submitted to the electorate at a regularly scheduled general election where
members of the local governing board are subject to election did not apply to taxes proposed
by voter initiative. The court categorized taxes imposed by citizen initiatives as separate from
taxes imposed by local governments. This ruling brought the two-thirds (66.67%) vote
requirement into question for special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives.

City and county o+icials in San Francisco argued that the court's 2017 decision meant that
a simple majority—not a two-thirds supermajority—was required for the approval of local
citizen initiatives, including tax measures that designate funds for speciﬁc purposes. Based
on those arguments, the city certiﬁed the measures as approved.

The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association ﬁled a lawsuit against the city and county in August
2018, stating that the Proposition C, a commercial rent tax for childcare initiative, did not
receive su+icient votes because it needed a two-thirds supermajority vote.

  Dylan Hoffman, Legislative Advocate, Shaw Yoder Antwih Schmelzer & Lange

Re:  Proposition 45 Memo

Summary
Proposition 45 is an initiative statute on the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot. Proposition
45 would overhaul the state’s landmark environmental review law, the California
Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The measure aims to help developers advance projects
they designate as “essential” more quickly and easily. It would impose a 365-day limit on
environmental reviews for those projects, including infrastructure like roads and bridges,
housing, schools, broadband and wildfire mitigation. It would also require courts to rule
within 270 days on lawsuits related to the environmental review law.

Path to the Ballot
In California state law, the core difference between a statewide ballot initiative and a
legislatively initiated ballot measure (often called a legislative referral) lies in how they
originate and qualify for the ballot. A ballot initiative bypasses the state government to be
driven entirely by citizens, whereas a legislatively initiated measure must be passed by the
California State Legislature before going to the voters.

Proposition 45 is a statewide ballot initiative, not a legislative referral.

Key Provisions
1. Expedited Review Timelines:
  o Lead agencies must issue a final decision and complete environmental impact
  assessments within 365 days for a complete application.
  o Negative declarations must be completed within 180 days; other determinations
  within 90 days.
  o Public comment periods are shortened to 15 days for Mitigated Negative
  Declarations and 30 days for Environmental Impact Reports (EIRs).
  o If deadlines are missed, applicants can request a public hearing, which must be
  completed and decided within 60 days.

2. Scope – Definition of Essential Projects:
   o  Housing projects (including residential, mixed-use, transitional, farmworker,
  student, senior, and group living accommodations, as well as conversions of
  commercial buildings to residential use).
  o  Water projects (construction, expansion, repair, or improvement of public water
  systems).
  o  Public health projects (medical treatment facilities).
  o  Public safety projects (first responder facilities, wildfire risk reduction).
  o  Transportation projects (planning, construction, maintenance, and operation of
  public streets and highways using fuel tax revenues).

Source: State Legislative Analyst’s Office

  3. Other Major Changes:
  o New pre-application screening for tribal cultural resources and changes to tribal
  consultation processes.
  o Applicants may propose a single project alternative for EIRs, rather than multiple
  alternatives.
  o Requires prevailing wages and project labor agreements for all essential projects,
  with special labor rules for housing.
  o Limits the grounds for legal challenges to defects in the environmental
  document.
  o Judicial review of challenges must be resolved within 270 days, with limited scope
  and remedies.
  o Prohibits extension of public comment periods except by court order.

  Projected State Fiscal and Operational Impact
  Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—
  potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially
